claims.statement: Pompeii’s excavated streets bring houses, shops, baths and theatres into the same view. They let us follow activities that often disappear behind accounts of emperors and wars. The eruption of Vesuvius buried the city in 79 CE. Its remains preserve evidence from different phases of the city’s life, not a record of every inhabitant.

claims.statement: Pompeii: 1 CE to 79 CE. 1–79 CE is an editorial window for the early imperial city, not its foundation date. The map uses UNESCO’s Pompeii component reference.

claims.statement: A house at Pompeii was converted into a fullery, where workers washed clothes and processed cloth. Vats occupied the former domestic spaces, and a terrace was used for drying. The archaeological park describes most of the workforce as enslaved. The building connects household architecture with demanding commercial labour.

claims.statement: Washing clothes at Pompeii: 79 CE to 79 CE. Snapshot of evidence preserved by the 79 CE eruption, not a one-year business or its opening date. Stephanus’s ownership is inferred from inscriptions; the identity of a body found at the entrance is not assumed. Map point locates Pompeii, not the individual workshop.

claims.statement: At the shop associated with Vetutius Placidus, customers could buy hot food and drinks from a masonry counter fitted with large jars. The house behind it was connected to the business. A shrine on the back wall included household protectors and the gods Mercury and Dionysus. Commerce, domestic space and religious practice met in one building.

claims.statement: A limestone writing surface from Deir el-Medina lists forty workers and records reasons for absence. They include illness, deaths in the family, house building and work for a superior. This was an administrative record, not a survey of everyone’s working life. It gives individual glimpses of the obligations and interruptions behind the royal tombs.

claims.statement: Why Egypt’s tomb workers missed work: 1279 BCE to 1213 BCE. Shown within Ramesses II’s reign. The museum description assigns the register to his Year 40, while its catalogue metadata gives c.1250 BCE. The discrepancy is unresolved; this broad window does not mean the register spans the reign. The text covers 280 days. No precise site coordinate has been inferred.
